newsitem.title: RWANDA: Returned Rwandan Hutus say they are living in fear.
newsitem.headline: Returned Rwandan Hutus say they are living in fear.

text.p: Many Rwandan Hutus who returned home from refugee camps in Tanzania and Zaire say they are facing poverty, harassment and murder as they try to rebuild their lives.

Juliette Ngatera, a primary school teacher who walked from Tanzania in December, said this week she regretted having come back to her house in Bicumbi commune, 60 km (38 miles) east of the capital Kigali.
"Life was better there. As a Hutu and a returned refugee there is no chance that I will find work, all we can do is work on the farm from dawn until dusk like slaves," she said.
"On top of that people here accuse us all of being killers and who knows what will happen to us."
In the last two months of last year, more than a million Hutu refugees streamed back home from camps in neighbouring Tanzania and Rwanda after more than two years in exile.
The Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 in fear of reprisals after the genocide of an estimated 800,000 minority Tutsis and Hutu moderates before Tutsi-led rebels seized power in Kigali.
The mass return prompted a new wave of violence the government blames on Hutu former troops and extremist militiamen who sneaked back into the country among the other refugees.
Targeted by the Hutu militiamen are genocide witnesses who could testify in court, as well as Tutsi civilians.
Returnees have been caught both in the backlash by the army against the insurgents and the anger of local people who blame refugees for killing friends and family during the genocide.
A report from the U.N. Human Rights Field Operation in Rwanda (HRFOR) last month said attacks on recent returnees had shown a marked increase, particularly in the east.

In the most recent recorded attack 21 Hutu returnees, 16 of them children, were shot dead in their homes near Kibungo 100 km (60 miles) east of Kigali. Frightened neighbours did not want to suggest any motive for the attack.
Hatreds run deep and possible reasons for revenge are many.
Few doubt that among the returnees are a large number of people who took part in the genocide.
At least 5,000 returned refugees have been arrested for alleged involvement at various levels, bringing the population of Rwanda's already over-crowded prisons to more than 90,000 people.
Special genocide courts have so far sentenced 11 to death.
But some returnees say they are falsely accused, either from malice or because their property has been taken over while they were living in exile.

"Anyone who is wealthy or educated risks being accused, and if you find someone else in your house when you return and ask them to leave it is asking for trouble," said Theophas Bizimana, a returnee from Zaire who is now staying with relatives.
Government programmes are unable to build houses fast enough to accomodate the arrivals, and hundreds of thousands of Tutsis who have returned since 1994, many after a generation in exile.

"Particularly large numbers of Tutsis moved into the east after 1994, but they now find themselves outnumbered three to one by the refugees. It is not surprising if there is fear and if it occasionally means violence," said a western aid worker.
